333:
The following words, terms and phrases, when used in this article, shall have the meanings ascribed to them in this section, except where the context clearly indicates a different meaning:
Functions means the beneficial roles that wetlands serve, including storage, conveyance, and attenuation of floodwater and stormwater; protection of water quality and reduction of erosion; habitat for wildlife, including rare and endangered species; food chain support for a variety of wildlife and aquatic life; educational, historical, and archaeological value protection; and scenic, aesthetic, and recreational amenities.
Generalized wetland map means said map, being a subset of the U.S. Department of the Interior National Wetlands Inventory Maps.
Hydric soils means soils that form as a result of saturated soil conditions. A listing of these soils is maintained by the Soil Conservation Service.
Hydrophytic vegetation means macrophytic plants tolerant of or dependent upon saturated soil conditions.
Jurisdictional determination means an official written statement or map signed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
Jurisdictional wetland means a wetland area that meets the definition requirements for the term "wetland," as determined by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
Regulated activity means any activity which will, or which may reasonably be expected to, result in the discharge of dredged or fill material into waters of the United States, except for those activities exempted in section 14-47(b) and exempted in section 404 of the Federal Clean Water Act.
Silviculture means the process of producing, reproducing, and growing a forest of distinctive stands of trees.
Temporary emergency permit means a temporary permit that may be issued in circumstances outlined in section 14-47(b)(8).
Wetland means an area that is inundated or saturated by surface water or groundwater at a frequency and distribution sufficient to support, and under normal circumstances does support, a prevalence of vegetation typically adapted for life in saturated soil conditions, commonly referred to as hydrophytic vegetation. The term "wetland" generally includes swamps, bogs, marshes, floodplains, and other similar areas.
Wetland delineation means the establishment of wetland boundaries by a representative of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers or other agent designated by the Corps.
Wetland protection district means all wetlands within the jurisdiction of the city which are designated on the generalized wetland map as "wetlands providing significant wildlife habitat and/or which may be subject to extensive mitigation."
(Ord. of 6-5-2000, § 10)
334:
(a) Findings of fact.
(1) The wetlands within the city are indispensable and fragile natural resources with significant development constraints due to flooding, erosion, and soil limitation. In their natural state, wetlands serve man and nature. They provide habitat areas for fish, wildlife and vegetation, water quality maintenance and control, flood control, erosion control, natural resources education, scientific study, open space, and recreational opportunities. In addition, the wise management of forested wetlands and adjacent floodplains is essential to the economic well-being of many communities within the state. A considerable number of these important natural resources have been lost or impaired by draining, dredging, filling, excavating, building, pollution and other acts. Damaging or destroying wetlands threatens public safety and welfare.
(2) The state department of natural resources and the state department of community affairs have determined that each local government with classified wetlands located within its jurisdiction must adopt a wetlands protection ordinance under the requirements of House Bill 215, Georgia's 1989 Growth Strategies legislation, and the rules promulgated thereunder. It is necessary for the city to ensure maximum protection for wetlands by discouraging development activities that may adversely impact wetlands.
(b) Title and purpose. This article shall be known as the "Wetland Protection Ordinance of Warrenton, Georgia." The purpose of this article is to promote the appropriate protection and use of wetlands, while taking into account varying ecological, economic development, recreational and aesthetic values. Activities which may damage wetlands should be located on upland sites to the greatest degree practicable as determined by the permitting process. The objective of this article is to protect the wetlands from alterations and encroachments which will significantly affect or reduce their primary functions for water quality, floodplain and erosion control, groundwater recharge, aesthetic nature, and wildlife areas and which will also comply with the requirements of federal and state laws related to wetland protection.
(Ord. of 6-5-2000, § 1)
335:
(a) Applicability. This article shall apply to all wetlands within the wetland protection district as defined herein and located within the jurisdiction of the city. The generalized wetland map adopted as part of this article, shows the general location of wetlands and should be consulted by persons contemplating activities in or near wetlands before engaging in a regulated activity. The generalized wetland map shall be on file in the office of the city clerk.
(b) Wetland protection district boundaries. The generalized wetland map is a general reference document and the boundaries on this map are an approximation. The purpose of the map is to alert developers and/or landowners, if they are contemplating any activity within proximity to a wetland, that they are required to contact the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for specific guidance as to whether a Section 404 Permit will be required prior to any scheduled activity. All specific delineations of wetland boundaries, as required by section 404 of the Clean Water Act, as amended, shall be determined by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
(Ord. of 6-5-2000, § 2)
336:
(a) Local development permit requirements. No regulated activity will be allowed in the wetland protection district without a development permit from the city. The issuance of a local development permit by the city clerk is contingent upon the recommendation of the city engineer and full compliance with the terms of this article and other state and federal regulations. All activities that are not exempted in subsection (b) of this section shall be prohibited without prior issuance of a local development permit. If the area proposed for development is located within 50 feet of the wetland protection district boundary, a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers letter stating either the Corps has no jurisdiction or a Section 404 Permit shall be required prior to the issuance of a city permit.
(b) Permissible uses. The following uses shall be allowed within the wetland protection district to the extent that they are not prohibited by any other federal, state or local law:
(1) Operations conducted during normal silvicultural activities, including minor dredge and fill associated with road construction, harvesting and reforestation practices, provided they meet the performance standards, and road construction best management practices required under section 404 of the Clean Water Act.
(2) Conservation or preservation of soil water, vegetation, fish, and other wildlife, provided they do not adversely impact the waters of the state or the United States in such a way that would require an individual Section 404 Permit.
(3) Outdoor passive recreational activities, including fishing, birdwatching, hiking, boating, horseback riding, and canoeing.
(4) Forestry practices applied in accordance with best management practices approved by the state forestry commission.
(5) The cultivation of agricultural crops. Agricultural activities shall be subject to the best management practices approved by the state department of agriculture.
(6) The pasturing of livestock, provided that riparian wetlands are protected, that the soil profile is not disturbed and that best management practices are followed.
(7) Education, scientific research, and natural trails.
(8) Temporary emergency permit. A temporary emergency permit may be issued by the city or its designee only for the following reasons:
a. Maintenance or repair of public roads or structures and for facilities in the service of the public which provide transportation, electrical, gas, water, sewer, telephone, telecommunications or other similar services, provided that such roads, structures or facilities are not enlarged, and that prior to the commencement of work, a written notice has been provided to the city. Said notice shall certify to the city that all work will be conducted using best management practices that will ensure that flow and circulation patterns and chemical and biological characteristics of the affected wetlands will not be impaired and all adverse impacts on the aquatic environment shall be minimized.
b. Temporary water level stabilization measures associated with silvicultural operations, provided that they are necessary to alleviate abnormally wet or dry conditions that would result in adverse impacts on the silvicultural activities if not corrected.
c. Limited ditching, tilling, dredging, excavating, or filling activities solely for the purpose of maintaining or repairing existing drainage systems critical for the cultivation of agricultural crops, provided that the proposed activities do not result in the impairment, alteration or destruction of wetlands.
d. Limited excavating and filling necessary for the repair and maintenance of piers, walkways, natural trails, observation decks, wildlife management shelters, boathouses, docks, and other similar water-related structures, provided that they are constructed on pilings to allow unobstructed flow of water and preserve the natural contour of the wetland.
(c) Site plans. All applications for a development permit within the generalized wetland protection district shall include a site plan, prepared by a registered engineer by the state, and drawn at a scale of one inch equals 50 feet, with the following information:
(1) Engineering drawings of all planned excavations and fill, including calculations of the volume of cut and fill involved, and cross-sectional drawings of existing and proposed grades. Elevations and horizontal and vertical scales must be shown on the cross-section drawings.
(2) Locations, dimensions and area of all impervious surfaces, both existing and proposed, on the site and adjacent to the site for a distance of ± 200 feet per state EPD standards.
(3) The orientation and distance from the boundaries of the proposed site to the nearest bank of an affected stream, river or water body.
(4) Elevations of the site and adjacent lands within 200 feet of the site at contour intervals of no greater than two feet.
(5) Locations and detailed designs of any spill or leak collection systems designed for the purpose of containing accidentally released hazardous or toxic materials.
(6) All proposed temporary disruptions or diversions of local hydrology.
(d) Activities to comply with site plan. All development activities or site work conducted after approval of the site plan by the city engineer shall conform with the specifications of said site plan. The site plan may be amended only with the approval of the city council. The city may require a performance bond up to $5,000.00 per acre of the project area and with surety and specific additional conditions adequate to secure compliance with all limitations set forth in the permit. The specific amount and conditions of the bond shall be determined by the city engineer and shall be consistent with the purposes of this article. In the event of a breach of condition of any such bond, the city shall collect such bond and/or institute the appropriate legal action in a court of competent jurisdiction upon such bond and prosecute the same to judgment and execution.
(e) Filing fee. At the time of the application, the applicant shall pay an initial filing fee per acre as provided in the city fee schedule. This fee will be used by the city to obtain professional engineering services to evaluate the application and determine the mitigation measures deemed necessary by the city. All additional city engineering costs beyond the filing fee shall be reimbursed to the city by the applicant prior to the issuance of a permit.
(f) Enforcement authority. The mayor and city council is hereby established as the administrator of this article.
(g) Review procedures. Three copies of the application shall be made to the city, one copy being forwarded to the city's designated engineer for review. Said review shall be completed by no later than 60 days in accordance with the provisions of the article. The engineer shall prepare a written evaluation report of the application and present written findings of approval or disapproval to the mayor and city council. The applicant shall also receive a copy of the written findings. The city has the right to extend the review period for an additional 30 days based upon specific concerns outlined to the city council by the engineer. If the application review is not completed within 90 days from the date of submission, the application is considered to be approved for the purposes of this application.
(h) Appeals. Decisions on any permit application by the city engineer may be appealed in writing within ten days to the city council. A public hearing shall be conducted within 30 days by the city for all appeals. A public announcement of the hearing shall be printed in the legal organ for the city at least 15 days prior to the hearing. Any person or interested party may offer testimony at the hearing. The final decision of the city council may be appealed to the court of competent jurisdiction as outlined in section 14-50.
(i) Duration of the permit validity.
(1) If construction described in the development permit has not commenced within six months from the date of issuance, the permit shall expire.
(2) If construction in the development permit is suspended or abandoned after work has commenced, the permit shall expire six months after the date the work has ceased.
(3) Written notification of the pending expiration of the development permit shall be issued by the city clerk by certified mail by no later than five working days of the expiration date.
(Ord. of 6-5-2000, § 3)

341:
Assessors and the board of assessors shall consider wetland regulations in determining fair market values of land. Any owner of an undeveloped wetland who has dedicated an easement or entered into a conservation restriction with the government or nonprofit organization to permanently control some or all regulated activities in the wetland shall have that portion of land assessed consistent with these restrictions. Such landowner shall also be exempted from any special assessment on the controlled wetland to defray the cost of municipal improvements such as sanitary sewers, storm sewers and water mains.
